title: The 14-Second Video
fiction_notice: All people, accounts and events in this file are invented.

post.caption: Have young people really forgotten how to respect their elders?
post.body: Footage shows a young woman shouting at an elderly passenger on the eastbound platform.

claims.text: The woman used aggressive language toward the older passenger.
claims.explanation: Evidence #01 records the language directly, and nothing here contradicts it — including the longer recording, which captures the same raised voice. This is the one part of the framing that survives contact with the evidence.
claims.note: This claim is narrow on purpose. It says what happened, not why, and not what it means.

claims.text: The woman verbally attacked the older passenger without provocation.
claims.explanation: The load-bearing word is “without provocation”. #04 and #08 both show the exchange was already underway before the recording began. The claim reaches further than the record.
claims.note: Unsupported is not the same as false. The evidence does not show the woman behaved well; it shows this particular claim reaches further than the record.

claims.text: This incident shows the woman is a generally ill-mannered person.
claims.explanation: One recorded minute can support a statement about what someone did. It cannot support a statement about who someone is.
claims.note: Watch for the moment a single action is quietly promoted into a description of a person.

claims.text: This incident shows young people are becoming less respectful toward their elders.
claims.explanation: One encounter cannot describe a generation. That step — from a single case to an entire age group — is one the evidence cannot make, whatever the clip shows.
claims.note: This is the same error as Claim C, one order of magnitude larger.

sources.label: Direct Accounts
sources.note: From people who were standing there

evidence.title: 14-Second Video
evidence.summary: The clip that started it. Fourteen seconds, no beginning, no end.
body: The recording begins mid-shout. A woman in her early twenties stands close to an older man. Her voice is raised and the words are unmistakably hostile.
The man does not step back. He says something the microphone does not pick up. The clip ends before he finishes.
proves: The woman used aggressive, insulting language.
The two were within arm’s reach of each other.
does_not_prove: What was said or done before the recording started.
Who started the exchange.
Anything about the woman beyond this moment.
evidence.analyst: Everything visible here is directly recorded — it does not depend on anyone’s account. What it cannot show is what came before: the clip has no start, and the first thing it captures is already a reaction.
evidence.hook: Notice that the clip has no beginning. Whatever started this happened off-camera.

evidence.title: Original Caption
evidence.summary: The sentence the uploader wrapped around the footage.
body: Posted with the video: “Have young people really forgotten how to respect their elders?”
It describes the platform, the people and the argument nowhere. It describes what the uploader wants the clip to mean.
proves: The uploader had a preferred reading of their own footage.
does_not_prove: Anything about what happened on the platform.
Whether the uploader believes the framing or is simply using it.
evidence.analyst: This is not a record of the event. It is a sentence someone wrote about the event. File it as evidence and you import the uploader’s conclusion before testing anything — which is the manoeuvre the whole incident is built on.
evidence.hook: A caption is a claim about evidence. It is not evidence.

evidence.title: Uploader Profile
evidence.summary: Who posted it, and what they post the rest of the week.
body: The account publishes confrontational footage several times a week — brief, unresolved, consistently without context.
Outrage-framed posts pull roughly four times the engagement of its calmer material. The pattern holds for months.
proves: The account has a commercial interest in outrage framing.
Short, context-free clips are its standard format, not an exception.
does_not_prove: That this clip was altered.
That the events in it did not happen.
evidence.analyst: A history of outrage framing is a reason to look harder at the clip. It is not, by itself, a reason to disbelieve it. Motivation to frame is not evidence of fabrication.
evidence.hook: You can distrust the poster and still accept the footage. Two separate questions.

evidence.title: 90-Second Video
evidence.summary: A second recording, from before the clip began.
body: Another passenger was already filming. In the earlier footage the man turns toward the woman and speaks to her at length.
By the time the fourteen-second clip begins, the exchange is already heated. Both voices are up.
proves: The argument was already underway before the viral clip started.
The woman’s raised voice is a response, not the opening move.
does_not_prove: That her language was acceptable.
What the argument was about.
Who was in the right.
evidence.analyst: The first material in the file that reaches behind the viral clip. The clip captured the middle of an argument, not its start — one fact that does more work than everything else here combined.
evidence.hook: The clip was not edited. It was simply too short — and that is often enough.

evidence.title: Woman’s Statement
evidence.summary: Her own account, given the following day.
body: She says the man had been insulting her for several minutes before she responded, and that she was on her way home from a late shift.
She does not deny the language in the clip.
proves: There is a first-person claim that the man spoke first.
She is not disputing the words the clip records.
does_not_prove: That her account is accurate.
That her response was proportionate to whatever preceded it.
evidence.analyst: Genuinely relevant — she is the only person who can describe what she experienced, and also the person most affected by how this is judged. So it is a claim to test, not a fact to file. Note what she does not do: she does not deny the clip.
evidence.hook: Testimony is evidence. It is not automatically true, and not automatically false.

evidence.title: Witness Statement
evidence.summary: Someone else who was standing there.
body: A passenger waiting two metres away says the two had been arguing for about a minute before anyone started filming.
They add a detail the woman’s statement leaves out: the man was shouting too.
proves: The man was also raising his voice.
does_not_prove: Who spoke first.
What the argument was about.
Whether either account of the dispute is accurate.
evidence.analyst: An independent account from someone with no visible stake. It corroborates the argument and adds what the woman’s statement leaves out. A witness who contradicts the person they are supporting is usually worth more attention than one who does not.
evidence.hook: This witness helps the woman and still contradicts part of her account.

evidence.title: Metro Staff Report
evidence.summary: What staff recorded when they reached the platform.
body: Staff were called after the argument drew attention. Their note records both parties as highly agitated on arrival, with no physical contact.
It does not attempt to establish who began it, and it does not repeat either party’s account.
proves: Both parties were agitated when staff arrived.
does_not_prove: Who started the argument.
What was said before staff arrived.
evidence.analyst: A record of what staff found on arrival, not of how the incident began. Its value is mostly what it rules out — no physical contact — and its honesty about what it cannot say.
evidence.hook: Authority does not make a document decisive. It only makes it a document.

evidence.title: CCTV Summary
evidence.summary: The station’s own cameras, covering the whole minute.
body: Station cameras cover the platform continuously, so this record does not depend on when anyone chose to start recording.
The summary shows the man speaking to the woman first and at length; the woman responding; both raising their voices; no physical contact at any point.
proves: The man spoke to the woman first.
The conflict ran about a minute before the clip began.
Both raised their voices. Neither touched the other.
does_not_prove: What the argument was about.
Whether either person behaved reasonably overall.
What either of them is like outside this minute.
evidence.analyst: The most complete record here. Because coverage is continuous, it does not inherit Evidence #01’s central weakness — that someone decided when to start filming. When a record is not shaped by a choice, it stops being framing and starts being evidence.
evidence.hook: As close to the whole minute as this file will get.

gaps.message: Everything you hold comes from footage someone chose when to start. No longer or continuous recording has been reviewed.
You have footage but no accounts. No statement from anyone who was standing on that platform is in your file.
You have not looked at who published this or why. Framing is not evidence, but an unexamined frame is a gap.
No official account has been reviewed. Staff records are rarely decisive, but they are usually honest about their own limits.

A.supported: Let us test the edges. Which single piece of evidence would you remove to make this claim fail, and would removing it change what the clip shows?
A.suspicious: What exactly is not holding together? The language itself is directly recorded, so whatever is troubling you may belong to a different claim than this one.
A.unsupported: This claim asserts only that aggressive language was used. If you are withholding support, what in the file suggests the language was something else?
A.insufficient: The file contains a recording of the moment in question. What would additional evidence have to show for you to move off “not enough”?

B.supported: Your judgment rests almost entirely on Evidence #01. Does a fourteen-second recording establish what happened before it started?
B.suspicious: You are treating this as doubtful without having decided which element fails. Is it the attack, or is it the word “without provocation”?
B.unsupported: That reading fits the record so far. Which single piece of evidence would move you back, and have you looked for it?
B.insufficient: Which specific point is the file unable to settle — that the attack occurred, or that nothing provoked it?

C.supported: You are moving from one recorded minute to a description of a person. What in the file speaks to her behaviour outside this incident?
C.suspicious: Even if the incident reflects badly on her, this claim asks whether it describes her generally. Is that the same question?
C.unsupported: You have withheld support. Is that because the evidence shows the opposite, or because it cannot reach that far?
C.insufficient: If more footage of this same argument arrived, would it close the gap? What kind of material would?

D.supported: The claim moves from one encounter to an entire age group. What in the file tells you about anyone other than the two people on that platform?
D.suspicious: Something about this claim is bothering you. Is the problem the size of the claim, or the evidence behind it?
D.unsupported: Good. Now be precise: is this claim defeated by contrary evidence, or simply beyond what any single case could support?
D.insufficient: Which is it — not enough evidence, or evidence that cannot apply at this scale?

debrief.title: Reasoning Debrief
debrief.lede: Not a score. A record of how your reading changed, and why.
debrief.closing: The clip was not faked. Nobody edited it. It was simply too short, published to be shared, and read as though it were the whole minute.
debrief.closing_note: Claims A and B differ by three words. Three words were enough to change a true statement into an unsupported one.

feedback.all_aligned: All four of your final judgments fall inside the range this file accepts. That is a reading of the claims, not a verdict on you. The two that carry weight are B and D — each fails on a single word or a single step, and both read as convincing right up until that word or step is named.
feedback.aligned_unseen: This claim matches the reading the file accepts — but the material that decides it was never opened. The answer can still be right; what is missing is the ability to say what would have changed it.

gloss.supported: The file contains material that establishes this, and nothing in it points the other way.
gloss.unsupported: The file does not carry this. That is not the same as the file showing the opposite — it means the claim asks for more than the record can give.
gloss.insufficient: The file neither establishes this nor rules it out. What is missing is the kind of material the claim would need to be answered either way.
gloss.suspicious: Something in the file leans against this, but not far enough to settle it.

unsupported.text: This claim is deliberately narrow: it says the language was used, and stops there. Evidence #01 records exactly that, and the longer recording #04 catches the same raised voice rather than contradicting it. Withholding support here asks the file to prove something it was never asked to prove.
unsupported.training: Separate what happened from why it happened. Claims about the bare event usually survive contact with the record; claims about motive usually do not.

insufficient.text: The claim does not ask what led to the exchange or who was in the right — only whether the words were spoken. Evidence #01 is a direct recording of that moment. More material would add context, not change what was said.
insufficient.training: Before calling something “not enough”, name what specifically is missing. If you cannot point at anything, the gap may be imaginary.

suspicious.text: Unease belongs to Claim B, not to A. The two differ by three words, and the words that fail are “without provocation”. Here the doubt lands on the part the recording actually captures.
suspicious.training: When a claim feels wrong, find the word doing the work. The doubt usually belongs to that word rather than to the whole sentence.

supported.text: The load-bearing phrase is “without provocation”. Evidence #04 and #08 both show the exchange was already underway before the recording began. Her tone may well have been aggressive — Claim A covers that — but this sentence asserts something the record actively works against.
supported.training: Read for the word the claim cannot survive without. Endorsing the sentence whole means accepting the part the evidence already contradicts.

insufficient.text: This is not a gap. Evidence #04 and #08 speak directly to the disputed point, and what they show runs against the claim. Calling it “not enough evidence” leaves “without provocation” standing after the file has already answered it.
insufficient.training: “Not enough evidence” and “the evidence points the other way” are different verdicts. Choosing the softer one still lets the wrong reading through.

suspicious.text: “Suspicious” records unease without naming it. Here the difficulty has a name: the exchange was already in progress when the recording started. A verdict you can state is more useful than one you can only feel.
suspicious.training: Turn unease into a sentence. If you can say what is wrong, say it — that is what a claim-level verdict is for.

supported.text: One recorded minute can support a statement about what someone did. It cannot support a statement about who they are. Nothing in the file describes this woman outside this single exchange, so the reading has no floor to stand on.
supported.training: Watch for the moment a single action is quietly promoted into a description of a person.

unsupported.text: “Unsupported” would mean the file leans against this. It does not lean either way — there is simply nothing in it about her character. That is a gap, and a gap is a different verdict from a contradiction.
unsupported.training: Distinguish “the file says no” from “the file does not say”. Both feel like rejection; only one is supported.

suspicious.text: Suspicion points at something present that does not hold together. Nothing about her character is present at all: the clip records one exchange, and character lies outside what it recorded.
suspicious.training: Check whether the evidence is thin or absent. Absent evidence calls for a different verdict than shaky evidence.

supported.text: One encounter cannot describe a generation. The step from a single case to an entire age group is one the evidence cannot take, whatever the clip shows.
supported.training: Notice when a claim grows its subject — from this person to a group, from now to a trend.

suspicious.text: This is the same step as Claim C, one order of magnitude larger. The file holds one recorded exchange; it says nothing about how young people in general behave, now or before.
suspicious.training: Size the subject to the evidence. One case can illustrate; it cannot describe.
